questions.q: What happens by default when a Salesforce record is deleted?
options: It is flagged as deleted and moved into the Recycle Bin, where it remains restorable for a documented 15-day window
It is immediately and permanently erased with no recovery option
It is automatically converted into a Big Object record
It is hidden from the owner but still visible to every other user
questions.explain: Salesforce's default delete behavior is a soft delete: the record moves to the Recycle Bin and stays restorable for 15 days before being scheduled for permanent removal.

questions.q: Why does a soft-deleted record still affect database performance even though it doesn't count against the org's storage limits?
options: Because storage limits and performance are entirely unrelated to Salesforce's architecture
Because soft-deleted records are automatically re-indexed every hour
Because the underlying data still physically exists while in the Recycle Bin, so queries still have to account for excluding it from results
Because the Recycle Bin uses a separate, slower database engine
questions.explain: Not counting toward storage and not affecting query performance are two different things — the record's data is still present during its Recycle Bin retention window, which still has a real cost on queries scanning the object.

questions.q: What distinguishes hard delete from the default soft-delete behavior?
options: Hard delete only works on standard objects, never custom objects
Hard delete is automatically triggered after exactly 15 days with no admin action
Hard delete is identical to soft delete but with a different error message
Hard delete removes a record immediately and permanently, bypassing the Recycle Bin entirely, and must be explicitly enabled since it's disabled by default
questions.explain: Hard delete bypasses the Recycle Bin stage and permanently removes the record immediately, available via Bulk API/Bulk API 2.0, but it's an administrator-enabled option, not the default behavior.

questions.q: At roughly what volume does Salesforce's own guidance recommend hard delete through Bulk API 2.0 specifically?
options: Any deletion of more than 10 records
On the order of a million or more records
Only when deleting fewer than 100 records at a time
Hard delete is never recommended at any volume
questions.explain: Salesforce's guidance points to roughly a million or more records as the point where hard delete through Bulk API 2.0 is the recommended approach, since the alternative would mean a large backlog of records cycling through a costly 15-day soft-delete window.

questions.q: Why is truncation described as a narrow, mainly sandbox-oriented tool rather than a general production deletion strategy?
options: Because truncation clears an entire custom object at once rather than a filtered set of records, requires Salesforce Support to execute, and can't be used if the org has already reached its custom-object limit
Because truncation is only available for standard objects like Account and Opportunity
Because truncation is identical to a hard delete and offers no distinct behavior
Because truncation automatically restores all deleted records after 24 hours
questions.explain: Truncation isn't a filtered bulk-delete operation — it clears an entire custom object immediately, needs Support assistance, and has its own constraint around the org's custom-object limit, which is why it's mainly used to clear sandbox test data rather than as a production deletion strategy.
